discovery.notes: The embedded star cluster NGC 2244 had already been found by John Flamsteed in 1690; the surrounding nebulosity itself eluded observers until Swift's survey.
Catalogued by Grigory Shajn and Vera Gaze in their survey of emission nebulae on Simeis Observatory plates.
Catalogued as Sh2-108 in Sharpless's survey of HII regions; surrounds the open cluster M6 (Butterfly Cluster).
Their looping tidal tails earned them the nickname 'Antennae'; the pair is a textbook example of a galaxy merger in progress.
A Wolf-Rayet bubble blown by the massive, rapidly-evolving star HD 56925.
First recorded on a photographic plate; too faint to have been seen visually before then.
Mechain found the Owl Nebula and the edge-on galaxy M108 within weeks of each other while sweeping for comets; they share a field by chance, at vastly different distances.

discovery.location: Cape of Good Hope, South Africa
discovery.notes: Catalogued by Lacaille during his survey of the southern sky; added to the Messier Catalog by Charles Messier in 1781.
Independently found by Johann Elert Bode a few weeks later the same year.
First recorded by Hodierna; independently catalogued by Charles Messier in 1764.
Described in al-Sufi's Book of Fixed Stars as a "little cloud"; first observed telescopically by Simon Marius in 1612.
Independently catalogued by Charles Messier in 1764; home of the 'Pillars of Creation'.
Mechain found M65 and M66 together; the third member, NGC 3628, was added by William Herschel in 1784.
The dark 'trunk' globule (vdB 142) sits within the much larger IC 1396 emission region and star cluster.
The visible remnant of a supernova that exploded roughly 10,000-20,000 years ago.
Known since antiquity to the naked eye; Galileo was the first to resolve dozens of additional stars with a telescope.
The first planetary nebula ever catalogued.
Heavily obscured by dust in the Milky Way's own disk, which is why it's nicknamed the 'Hidden Galaxy' despite being relatively close and intrinsically bright.
Too faint and diffuse to appreciate visually; its North-America shape wasn't obvious until Max Wolf's wide-field photographs in the 1890s.

name: C 12 & Barnard 150 (Fireworks Galaxy & Dark Sea Horse Nebula)

discovery.notes: NGC 6946 ('Fireworks Galaxy', nicknamed for its unusually high supernova rate) was found by Herschel; the dark nebula Barnard 150 was catalogued decades later by E. E. Barnard from photographic plates in his Atlas of Selected Regions of the Milky Way.
One member, NGC 7320, is actually a much closer foreground galaxy; the other four form the true physically interacting group.
Markarian identified these Virgo Cluster galaxies as a physically related chain by their shared proper motion.
Usually credited as the first telescopic observer of the nebula itself, a few months after Galileo's first telescopic observations of the sky.
Its three dark dust lanes, which give the nebula its name, were first described by John Herschel in the 1830s.
Independently catalogued by Charles Messier in 1764.
Found by Caroline Herschel while sweeping for comets, one of several discoveries credited to her independently of her brother William.
Part of the same star-forming complex as the neighboring Heart Nebula (IC 1805).
Catalogued as Abell 426; one of the most massive nearby galaxy clusters, with a hot intracluster medium studied extensively in X-rays.
Independently rediscovered by Charles Messier in 1758, prompting him to begin the Messier Catalog.
